1401.title: Processions
1401.hook: Holy Week in Seville, Corpus Christi in villages: faith in the streets
1401.howItsDone: Catholics walk in procession with palms on Palm Sunday and, in some places, follow the Eucharist through the streets on Corpus Christi. In Seville and elsewhere in Spain, lay brotherhoods carry images of Christ and Mary through the streets during Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Day of the Dead: a photograph, a candle, marigolds in a path to the door. Your line was they're remembered.

Late at night in a narrow street in Seville, during Holy Week. The crowd is packed so tight nobody can turn around. Then a slow drum, and a hush. Around the corner sways a huge wooden platform, lit by rows of candles, carrying a figure of Christ bent under his cross. The bearers are hidden underneath, shoulders to the beams, moving in step to a voice calling from outside. In front walk long lines of penitents in robes and tall pointed hoods, holding candles. A woman on a balcony sings a short, raw song to the figure as it passes.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT IN SEVILLE.` → `A PLATFORM CARRIED BY HIDDEN BEARERS.` → `A SONG FROM A BALCONY.`

segments.voice: Start with a crowd on a road. As Jesus rides into Jerusalem, people spread cloaks and cut branches, walking ahead and behind him, shouting. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." You met that road in your first year, and on Palm Sunday Catholics repeat the walk with branches in hand. A procession is faith that moves. Next, Seville. In Holy Week its brotherhoods, lay associations of Catholics, carry images of Christ and Mary through the streets. The pointed hoods are penitents' hoods. Tradition says they hide the face so the penance is offered without anyone knowing who is doing it. The bearers underneath are hidden too. The whole thing is built so the images are seen and the people aren't. Then a quieter scene. On Corpus Christi, the priest carries the Eucharist in a monstrance, under a canopy, through a parish or village. In some villages people lay carpets of flower petals and colored sawdust for it to pass over, carpets trampled in minutes. Church law asks for a public procession on this feast where it can be done, as a public witness of reverence. Last, why walk at all? A church building holds faith still. A procession takes it out the door, past the bakery and the bus stop, and says, without a sermon, that God isn't only indoors, and that the Church is a people on the move, walking somewhere together.
screen: `HOSANNA ON THE ROAD.` · `SEVILLE: HIDDEN FACES, SEEN IMAGES.` · `CORPUS CHRISTI OVER FLOWER CARPETS.` · `GOD ISN'T ONLY INDOORS.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you can, step outside or walk to a window, and notice the street: who passes, what's open, what you hear. Take a few slow steps in time with your breath, as if in a procession; if you can't move today, let your eyes do the walking. If you pray, say the Hosanna line quietly or carry someone in your prayer; if you don't, carry a good wish for each person you see.
Processions. The Church walking together through the streets with branches, images or the Eucharist: on Palm Sunday, in Holy Week, on Corpus Christi. Today's word.
Your line: faith in the streets. A small procession of one still counts. See you tomorrow.

1402.title: Bells
1402.hook: church bells call to Mass, ring the Angelus and toll for the dead
1402.howItsDone: Catholic parishes may ring a bell before Mass, and some still ring the Angelus in the morning, at noon and in the evening, when people who hear it may stop to pray it. Bells are tolled for funerals, a small bell may be rung at the consecration, and the bells fall silent from the Gloria of Holy Thursday until the Gloria of the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, processions: a statue, a candle, a crowd, and the church walking out its own front door. Your line was faith in the streets.

Noon on a weekday. In a town square, a bell starts up in the church tower: a few strokes, a pause, a few more. A woman at a café table sets her cup down. A man unloading a van stops, a box in his arms. Others keep walking. The bell rings either way. The painter Jean-François Millet caught that moment in a field, in a canvas called The Angelus: two farm workers, a pitchfork and a basket at their feet, heads bowed while a far-off steeple rings. A bell can't say a single word. It can only call.
screen: `NOON. A BELL IN THE TOWER.` → `A CUP SET DOWN.` → `IT CAN ONLY CALL.`

segments.voice: You met the Angelus prayer back on day one hundred three. In a Catholic parish, the bell has jobs. It calls people to Mass: when it rings before the liturgy, everyone in earshot knows the doors are open. It rings the Angelus, named for the prayer's first Latin words, Angelus Domini, the angel of the Lord. The prayer walks through the Annunciation, with Mary's words at its heart, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Then a line from John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Tradition rings it morning, noon and evening, so an ordinary day gets stitched, again and again, to the moment God came close. And it tolls for the dead. Slow strokes, spaced far apart, tell the street that someone has died or is being buried. Nobody has to post a notice; the neighbors know to pray. There's a smaller bell inside, too. The Church's instructions for Mass allow a server to ring it just before the consecration, and again as the priest lifts the host and then the chalice. Heads come up. Then there's the week the bells go quiet. On Holy Thursday they ring out during the Gloria, and after that the Missal has them fall silent, all through Good Friday. They come back at the Easter Vigil, when the Gloria is sung again. For a few days, the silence does the calling.
screen: `A BELL CALLS PEOPLE TO MASS.` · `THE ANGELUS: THE WORD MADE FLESH.` · `A SLOW TOLL FOR THE DEAD.` · `SILENT FROM HOLY THURSDAY TO EASTER.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Let the app's bell be your church bell: when it sounds, stop whatever your hands were about to do, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, say the Angelus, or only Mary's line, be it done to me according to thy word. If you don't, simply notice where you are, who is near, and what this hour is holding.
Bells. In a Catholic parish, the sound that calls people to Mass, rings the Angelus, and tolls for the dead, and that falls silent from Holy Thursday until Easter. Today's word.
Your line: the bell calls. It can't say a word, and still the whole street knows what it means. Until tomorrow.

1403.title: Monica's Saturday fast
1403.hook: veils, kneeling, silence or sung responses: customs differ from parish to parish
1403.tomorrow: Two forms of the Latin rite
1403.howItsDone: Catholic customs at Mass vary by country and parish: some women wear a chapel veil and others don't, bishops' conferences adapt when the people kneel or stand, and parishes differ in music, language and silence. Visitors are generally expected to follow the custom of the parish they're in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bells: the Angelus at noon, the slow toll for the dead. Your line was the bell calls.

A lace veil, folded small, lives in the coat pocket of a woman who travels for work. One Sunday, in one city, she puts it on, and so do several women around her. The next Sunday, in another city, she's the only one, and she wonders whether to take it off. In the first church the people kneel after the Lamb of God; in the second they stand until communion. One choir chants the responses in Latin; across town, a guitar leads them in English. One parish keeps a long silence after communion; another goes straight to the announcements. Same Mass. Same creed. Is somebody doing it wrong?
screen: `A VEIL IN A COAT POCKET.` → `KNEEL HERE, STAND THERE.` → `IS SOMEBODY DOING IT WRONG?`

segments.voice: Saint Augustine tells an old version in one of his letters. His mother, Monica, had moved to Milan, and she was troubled: back home she had fasted on Saturdays, and in Milan the church didn't. Augustine asked the bishop of Milan, Ambrose. His answer, as Augustine reports it: when I'm here, I don't fast on Saturday; when I'm in Rome, I do. Follow the custom of the church you're in. Augustine says he took that answer as if it had come from heaven. Writing to the Romans, who were arguing about food and holy days, he says in the Douay-Rheims: "One judgeth between day and day: and another judgeth every day: let every man abound in his own sense." Then he tells them to stop judging each other. The Church draws a line between what is shared and what is local. The faith, the sacraments, the heart of the Mass: these are one. The Second Vatican Council said the Church doesn't want a rigid sameness in matters that don't touch the faith or the good of the whole community. The instructions for Mass let each country's bishops adapt postures, and leave room for music, language and local devotion. So a veil worn by choice, a kneel or a stand, a chant or a hymn, can differ and both be faithful. And customs carry love: a grandmother's mantilla, a parish's long silence. The question isn't whose custom wins. It's whether you can kneel beside someone else's.
screen: `MONICA'S QUESTION IN MILAN.` · `AMBROSE: FOLLOW THE CHURCH YOU'RE IN.` · `PAUL: LET EVERY MAN ABOUND.` · `ONE FAITH, LOCAL CUSTOMS.` · then, large: `LET EVERY MAN ABOUND IN HIS OWN SENSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a church habit that isn't yours, a veil, a raised hand, and one real person who keeps it. Ask what it might hold for them: a memory, a family, a way of saying yes to God. If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, wish them well in the thing they love.
Many customs. The Catholic understanding that one faith and one Mass can be kept with different local habits: veils, postures, music and silence. Today's word.
Your line: one faith, many local customs. One faith can kneel in more than one way. Go gently.

1404.title: Two forms of the Latin rite
1404.word: Two forms of the Latin rite
1404.hook: the Mass of 1970 and the older Latin Mass both have devoted followers, with strong feelings
1404.howItsDone: Latin Catholic parishes celebrate the Mass in the reformed Roman Missal, usually in the local language; some communities, with their bishop's permission, celebrate the older Latin Mass. Catholics may attend either, and both are celebrated as the one sacrifice of the Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many customs: Ambrose telling Monica to follow the church she was in. Your line was many customs.

Two friends meet for brunch after Sunday Mass. They went to different churches. One went to a Mass in English: the priest facing the people across the altar, the whole room singing the responses, his opening words in her own language. The other went to a Latin Mass: chant, long silences, the priest facing the same way as the people, toward the altar, beginning at its foot with a psalm in Latin. Both love what they went to. Both have, at some point, said something sharp about the other's. Neither of them is leaving the Church.
screen: `BRUNCH AFTER TWO MASSES.` → `ENGLISH AND SINGING. LATIN AND CHANT.` → `BOTH LOVE WHAT THEY WENT TO.`

segments.voice: After the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul VI issued a revised Roman Missal: the Mass in the reformed books, usually in the local language. The older Missal, used before the reform, gives the Latin Mass. It opens with prayers at the foot of the altar, built on a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "I will go in to the altar of God: to God who giveth joy to my youth." Some drawn to the older Mass speak of reverence, silence, and continuity with the generations who prayed it. Some drawn to the reformed Mass speak of hearing the readings in their own tongue, a wider sweep of scripture, and joining aloud in the prayers. The popes have handled this differently. Pope Benedict XVI widened permission for the older Mass and described the two as two expressions of the one Roman rite. Pope Francis later placed the older Mass under each bishop's oversight and taught that the reformed books are the one expression of the Roman rite's law of prayer. Some Catholics on each side have felt each decision deeply. Here is what both Masses share: the same sacrifice of Christ, made present; the same Gospels proclaimed; the same Lord received in communion. And one prayer prayed in both: the old Roman Canon, kept in the reformed Missal as the first Eucharistic Prayer. Paul begged a divided church in Corinth, in the Douay-Rheims, "that there be no schisms among you." Strong feelings, held by people who are in one Church.
screen: `THE REFORMED MISSAL AFTER THE COUNCIL.` · `THE OLDER MASS: TO THE ALTAR OF GOD.` · `TWO POPES, TWO DECISIONS.` · `ONE SACRIFICE, ONE ROMAN CANON.` · then, large: `THAT THERE BE NO SCHISMS AMONG YOU.`

Two forms of the Latin rite. The reformed Mass from after the Second Vatican Council and the older Latin Mass: both Roman, both offering the one sacrifice, both deeply loved. Today's word.

1405.title: Charismatic renewal (1967)
1405.hook: a movement of praise and gifts of the Spirit that began at a student retreat
1405.howItsDone: Catholics in the charismatic renewal gather in prayer groups, often in parish halls, for songs of praise, scripture, spontaneous prayer and sometimes praying in tongues, and they pray for a renewal of the Holy Spirit's gifts first given in baptism and confirmation. Other Catholics take no part, and both are fully part of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two forms of the Latin rite: one Roman Canon, prayed in both, and strong feelings on every side. Your line was one church, both loved.

A weekend retreat house outside Pittsburgh. College students from Duquesne University have come to pray, reading the opening chapters of the Acts of the Apostles: the wind and the fire at Pentecost. Their question is simple and a little dangerous: could that still happen? By the movement's own telling, on the Saturday night some of them wandered into the chapel, one by one, and didn't come out for a long time. They prayed, they praised; some wept, some laughed. Nobody had planned it. Out of that weekend, people say, a movement spread through the Catholic Church.
screen: `A STUDENT RETREAT, READING ACTS.` → `COULD THAT STILL HAPPEN?` → `INTO THE CHAPEL, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with the page they were reading. At Pentecost, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they began to speak with divers tongues, according as the Holy Ghost gave them to speak." The renewal takes that as more than a memory. Its members pray, in their own words, for the Spirit to stir up what was already given in baptism and confirmation. They call it being baptized in the Spirit, and they're careful to say it isn't a new sacrament. The name comes from charisms, the gifts of grace Paul lists for Corinth: wisdom, knowledge, healing, prophecy, tongues and more. And he insists, "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit." The Catechism takes Paul's line: charisms are graces given for building up the Church, to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church's pastors. What does it look like? A prayer meeting in a parish hall. Songs of praise, some hands raised, a reading, a long stretch of people praising God aloud in their own words, sometimes praying in tongues, then quiet. For some Catholics this is home. Others pray in silence and find it strange. Both are in the same Church. And Paul set a guardrail for an enthusiastic church: "Let all things be done decently, and according to order." Praise, with the Church's order around it. One short line runs through its prayer meetings: come, Holy Spirit.
screen: `PENTECOST: FILLED WITH THE HOLY GHOST.` · `CHARISM: A GIFT OF GRACE.` · `A PRAYER MEETING IN A PARISH HALL.` · `DECENTLY, AND ACCORDING TO ORDER.` · then, large: `DIVERSITIES OF GRACES, BUT THE SAME SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Praise is different from asking and from thanks: it names what someone is, not what they've done for you. If you pray, praise God in your own plain words, one name or one quality at a time, beginning the way the renewal does: come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, name things that are good simply because they are: light, a voice you love, water.
Charismatic renewal. A Catholic movement of praise that asks the Holy Spirit to stir up the gifts of grace Paul called charisms. Today's word.
Your line: come, spirit. With today, this stretch on devotions closes. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1406.title: Everyone has a vocation
1406.hook: vocation means calling, and every baptized person has one
1406.howItsDone: Catholics speak of a universal call to holiness that every baptized person shares, and of particular vocations: marriage, the single life, religious life and holy orders. Parishes pray for vocations, and people discerning a calling often talk it through with a priest, sister or spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, charismatic renewal: students reading Acts, and Paul's gifts of grace, the charisms. Your line was come, spirit.

It's night in the house of God at Shiloh. A boy named Samuel is asleep near the ark. A voice says his name. He runs to the old priest, Eli: here I am, you called me. Eli says he didn't; go back to bed. It happens again. Then the text says the Lord called Samuel again the third time, and this time Eli understands. If it comes again, he tells the boy, answer. It comes. And Samuel says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." A whole life starts with a name said in the dark. Today, a new stretch on callings.

segments.voice: Back on day six hundred sixty-seven, Good Shepherd Sunday, you met the Church's day of prayer for vocations. A vocation is a calling: not first a job or a career, but a voice, and somebody answering it. Praying for vocations can sound like praying only for priests, sisters and brothers. That's a real calling, and this stretch will get to it. But the Church's teaching starts wider. The Second Vatican Council said that all the faithful, whatever their state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of love. The Catechism repeats it: the call to holiness is for everyone. It goes back to a hard sentence of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect." Not said to monks: Matthew says the crowds heard it. So the Catholic picture has two layers. The first call comes to every baptized person, the same for all: to holiness, to love. Then each life answers it in a particular shape: marriage, the single life, religious vows, holy orders. Paul, writing from prison to a whole church of ordinary people, puts the first layer plainly: "I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you that you walk worthy of the vocation in which you are called." So the nurse on a night shift, the dad at school pickup, the student cramming: none of them is waiting for a calling to arrive someday. Catholic teaching says they already have one, and they're living it, or not, right now.
screen: `A VOCATION IS A CALLING.` · `NOT ONLY PRIESTS AND SISTERS.` · `ONE CALL TO HOLINESS FOR ALL.` · `THEN A SHAPE FOR EACH LIFE.` · then, large: `WALK WORTHY OF THE VOCATION IN WHICH YOU ARE CALLED.`

segments.voice: Not the next five years: who is in front of you this season, needing something only you can give? Let one face, or one task, come up and stay with it. If you pray, borrow Samuel's words, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth; if you don't, let the question sit, unanswered for now.
Vocation. A calling. In Catholic teaching, every baptized person's call to holiness, lived out in a particular state of life. Today's word.
Your line: called. The first call is the same for everyone: holiness, love. See you tomorrow.

1407.title: Marriage as calling
1407.hook: spouses become holy through each other
1407.howItsDone: Catholics marry in a wedding, within Mass or a liturgy of the word, where the couple exchange vows before a priest or deacon and witnesses. In the Latin Church the spouses are the ministers of the sacrament; in the Eastern Catholic churches the priest is, and he crowns the couple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vocation: Samuel hearing his name in the dark, and the Church saying everyone is called to holiness. Your line was called.

A Catholic wedding. The priest at the front in white vestments, the families in the pews, a cousin filming on a phone. The couple turn to each other and say their vows. One detail: in the Latin Church's teaching, the priest isn't the one giving this sacrament. The bride and groom are. They give it to each other. The priest, or a deacon, is there as the Church's witness, to receive their consent and to bless them. Then the reception, and home, and the real work starts the next morning, with dishes in the sink.
screen: `A WEDDING. A PRIEST IN WHITE.` → `THE COUPLE GIVE THE SACRAMENT.` → `THEN, THE NEXT MORNING.`

segments.voice: At the start of the Bible, the Lord God looks at the first man and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself." Not a servant: a help like himself. Then Paul, writing to the Ephesians, sets a very high bar: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the church, and delivered himself up for it." And he steps back from his own words: "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church." Paul's word there is mystery, and the Latin Bible rendered it sacramentum. For Catholics, a marriage between baptized people is a sacrament: a sign that does what it shows. The Catechism says that in the Latin Church the spouses themselves are the ministers, giving the sacrament to each other by their consent. The Eastern tradition sees it differently: there, the priest who crowns the couple is the minister. Both are Catholic. Then the calling. The Second Vatican Council said spouses help one another to holiness in their married life. Not in spite of each other: through each other. The person who knows how you load a dishwasher, and how you sound when you're tired, is the one who asks you, again and again, to forgive and to give. Every small yes counts as part of the vocation. That's the strange claim: a marriage isn't a break from the call to holiness. It's one of the shapes the call can take.
screen: `NOT GOOD FOR MAN TO BE ALONE.` · `AS CHRIST LOVED THE CHURCH.` · `THE COUPLE ARE THE MINISTERS.` · `HOLINESS THROUGH EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `THIS IS A GREAT SACRAMENT.`

segments.voice: If you're married, bring your spouse to mind as they really are today, not at the wedding; if not, a couple you know, maybe a marriage that's struggling, at their kitchen table. If you pray, ask God to make them holy through each other, and name them. If you don't, hold them in mind and wish them patience, laughter, and one easy evening.
Marriage as calling. In Catholic teaching, a vocation and a sacrament in which the spouses help each other toward holiness. Today's word.
Your line: holy through each other. The week ran from processions and bells to vocation and now marriage. Until tomorrow.
